Abortion was adopted as the movement's signature issue later, partly because it was a more morally persuasive rallying point than the defense of segregated schools.

Jerry Falwell's Moral Majority, founded in 1979, was the organizational vehicle for the political mobilization of conservative Protestants. Its agenda was explicitly political: opposition to abortion, opposition to the Equal Rights Amendment, support for prayer in public schools, and a robust Cold War anti-communism. Falwell was not subtle about his goals: "The idea that religion and politics don't mix was invented by the Devil to keep Christians from running their own country," he declared.

The alliance between evangelicalism and the Republican Party, consolidated during the Reagan era, transformed both. The Republican Party gained a reliable, highly motivated voting bloc. Evangelicalism gained political influence but at the cost of identifying the gospel with a particular political platform. The theological claim that Jesus is Lord — a claim with radical implications for every political order — was domesticated into the political claim that Christian values aligned with conservative Republican policies. The prophetic distance that the church is supposed to maintain from all earthly powers was collapsed into partisan loyalty.

The Prosperity Gospel

No development in American Christianity is more revealing of the tradition's accommodation to American culture than the prosperity gospel — the teaching that God wants believers to be financially wealthy, physically healthy, and personally successful, and that faith, positive speech, and financial giving are the means to obtain these blessings.

The movement's roots lie in the post-World War II healing revival, particularly in the ministry of Oral Roberts, who combined Pentecostal healing with a message of divine prosperity. Kenneth Hagin, a Pentecostal pastor in Texas, provided the theological framework through what he called the "Word of Faith" teaching: the spoken word has creative power, and believers who "name it and claim it" can materialize divine blessings through the force of their declarations.

The theology, such as it is, draws on a selective reading of scripture. Deuteronomy 28 promises material blessings for obedience. Malachi 3:10 promises that God will "open the windows of heaven" for those who tithe. 3 John 2, in the King James Version, expresses the wish that the reader may "prosper and be in health." The prosperity teachers treat these texts as unconditional promises, ignoring the vast weight of biblical testimony — from Job to the Psalms to the teachings of Jesus himself — that contradicts the equation of faithfulness with material success.

Joel Osteen, the pastor of Lakewood Church in Houston (the largest congregation in the United States, meeting in a former basketball arena), represents the prosperity gospel in its most polished contemporary form. Osteen's sermons are relentlessly positive, theologically thin, and laser-focused on personal success. "God wants you to be a winner, not a whiner," he told his congregation. The cross, the resurrection, sin, repentance, justice — these themes are largely absent from Osteen's preaching, replaced by a therapeutic optimism that owes more to Norman Vincent Peale and the American self-help tradition than to the apostle Paul.

The prosperity gospel is, in the most precise sense, a heresy — a distortion of the Christian message so fundamental that it constitutes a different religion. It inverts the gospel's logic: where Jesus said "Blessed are the poor," the prosperity teachers say "Blessed are the rich." Where Paul boasted of his weaknesses, the prosperity teachers boast of their private jets. Where the early church shared its possessions, the prosperity churches extract wealth from their congregations — often from the poorest and most vulnerable members — and concentrate it in the hands of celebrity pastors. It is the American gospel par excellence: faith as investment strategy, God as cosmic ATM, the church as spiritual marketplace.

Megachurch Culture and the Consumer Model

The megachurch — defined as a Protestant congregation with two thousand or more weekly attendees — is a distinctly American phenomenon, and its growth over the past four decades tells us as much about American consumer culture as about American religion. There are roughly 1,750 megachurches in the United States today, and their combined weekly attendance exceeds the population of many major cities.

The megachurch model, pioneered by figures like Robert Schuller (Crystal Cathedral), Bill Hybels (Willow Creek), and Rick Warren (Saddleback), applied the principles of marketing, consumer research, and organizational management to the life of the church. Hybels famously surveyed unchurched people in the suburbs of Chicago, asking them why they did not attend church, and then designed a worship experience that addressed their objections: no guilt, no religious jargon, no pressure to give money, professional-quality music, practical sermons on felt needs, and ample parking. The "seeker-sensitive" model was, in many respects, a work of organizational genius. It drew enormous crowds.

The theological question is whether the crowds were drawn to the gospel or to a consumer experience that happened to be located in a building called a church. The megachurch model assumes that the church must compete with other leisure and entertainment options for people's time and attention. The music must be as good as a concert. The children's programs must rival theme parks. The coffee must be excellent. The parking must be convenient. The implicit theology is that people are consumers and the church is a provider of religious goods and services.

This is a long way from the house churches of the first century, from the desert fathers, from the Anabaptist communities that met in barns and caves under threat of execution. Whether it is a legitimate adaptation of an ancient faith to modern conditions or a fatal capitulation to the forces of consumerism is a question that American Christianity has not yet honestly confronted.

Where American Christianity Stands Today

American Christianity in the third decade of the twenty-first century is fractured, politicized, and declining. The share of Americans who identify as Christian has fallen from 90 percent in the 1970s to roughly 64 percent in recent surveys. The "nones" — people who claim no religious affiliation — have grown from 5 percent to nearly 30 percent. Mainline Protestantism has been in freefall for half a century. Evangelicalism, long assumed to be immune to decline, has begun to show the same symptoms.

The causes are multiple and debated. The association of Christianity with right-wing politics has alienated younger Americans, particularly on issues of LGBTQ rights and racial justice. The clergy sex abuse scandals — not only in the Catholic Church but increasingly in Protestant denominations — have shattered the moral authority of institutional religion. The rise of digital culture has created alternative communities and meaning-making systems that compete with traditional religious participation. And the internal contradictions of American Christianity — its accommodation to consumerism, its alliance with political power, its racial segregation (Martin Luther King Jr.'s observation that eleven o'clock on Sunday morning is the most segregated hour in America remains substantially true) — have produced a credibility crisis from which the tradition may not recover.

The deepest problem, however, is theological. American Christianity has, over four centuries, so thoroughly absorbed American values — individualism, pragmatism, optimism, consumerism, nationalism — that it has become difficult to distinguish the faith from the culture. When the faith and the culture are indistinguishable, the faith has nothing distinctive to offer. It becomes, in the words of the theologian H. Richard Niebuhr, "a God without wrath who brought men without sin into a Kingdom without judgment through the ministrations of a Christ without a Cross."

The question facing American Christianity is not whether it will survive — some form of it certainly will. The question is whether it can recover a faith robust enough to challenge the culture that has domesticated it. This would require, at minimum, a willingness to disentangle the gospel from American nationalism, to recover a theology of suffering and sacrifice in a culture of comfort and success, to practice genuine racial reconciliation in the most racially divided institution in American life, and to rediscover the prophetic tradition that speaks truth to power rather than seeking proximity to it.

Whether American Christianity has the theological resources and the institutional will to undertake this recovery is the most important religious question of the twenty-first century. The history surveyed in this article offers both hope and warning. The American tradition has produced genuine theological brilliance (Edwards, the Niebuhrs, King), extraordinary institutional creativity (the voluntary denomination, the parachurch organization, the historically Black church), and a commitment to religious liberty that, at its best, has been a gift to the world. But it has also produced theological superficiality, cultural captivity, racial injustice, and a confusion of faith with national identity that has distorted the gospel beyond recognition.

The path forward is not back — not to the Puritans, not to the revivals, not to the Christian America that never quite existed. The path forward requires a reckoning with the full weight of the tradition: its achievements and its failures, its insights and its blind spots, its prophets and its profiteers. American Christianity became American. The question now is whether it can become Christian again.
excerpt: The story of how a transplanted European faith became something entirely new — shaped by revivalism, individualism, capitalism, and a national mythology that confused the kingdom of God with the United States of America.

title: The Rise and Fall of Mainline Protestantism
body:
If you had attended a suburban church in the United States in 1955, there is a strong chance it would have been a mainline Protestant congregation. The minister would have been educated at a reputable seminary. The hymnal would have been vetted by denominational committees. The congregation would have included bankers, schoolteachers, lawyers, and local politicians. The church building itself would have been architecturally substantial, set prominently on a main street. And the theology preached from the pulpit, while perhaps not systematic, would have carried the quiet confidence of a tradition that believed it spoke for the nation.

That world is gone. Not destroyed by persecution or suppressed by the state, but eroded from within and overtaken from without. The story of mainline Protestantism's rise and fall is one of the most consequential narratives in American religious history, and most Americans have never heard it told clearly.

What "Mainline" Actually Means

The term "mainline" refers to a cluster of Protestant denominations that dominated American religious and civic life from the colonial era through the mid-twentieth century. The label itself derives from the "Main Line," a stretch of affluent suburbs along the Pennsylvania Railroad west of Philadelphia, where these churches were as much a part of the social landscape as the country clubs and prep schools. The term was not originally theological. It was sociological. These were the churches of the American establishment.

The so-called "Seven Sisters" of mainline Protestantism are the United Methodist Church, the Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.), the Episcopal Church, the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America, the United Church of Christ, the Christian Church (Disciples of Christ), and the American Baptist Churches USA. Together, these denominations and their predecessors constituted the institutional spine of American Protestantism for more than two centuries.

Their influence extended far beyond Sunday worship. Mainline Protestants founded the majority of America's elite universities: Harvard, Yale, Princeton, Columbia, Dartmouth, and dozens more. They built hospitals, orphanages, and settlement houses. They shaped public school curricula. Their clergy were invited to pray at presidential inaugurations. Their moral assumptions saturated American law, literature, and manners. To be "mainline" was to be the religious expression of the American middle and upper-middle class, with all the privilege and blind spots that entailed.

The Ecumenical Vision

One of the mainline's most distinctive contributions was its commitment to ecumenism, the effort to overcome denominational division and pursue Christian unity. The Federal Council of Churches, founded in 1908, brought mainline denominations together for cooperative social witness decades before evangelicals developed comparable institutions. The World Council of Churches, established in Amsterdam in 1948, represented the global extension of this vision, an institutional expression of the conviction that Christian division was a scandal to be overcome rather than a tradition to be defended.

This ecumenical impulse was rooted in a specific theological conviction: that denominational boundaries were historical accidents rather than divine mandates. The prayer of Jesus in John 17, "that they may all be one," was taken not as a pious aspiration but as a programmatic directive. Mainline theologians argued that a divided church could not credibly proclaim a gospel of reconciliation. The fragmentation of Protestantism into thousands of competing denominations was, on this view, a failure of nerve and an obstacle to mission.

The ecumenical movement produced landmark achievements. The Consultation on Church Union (1962) brought ten denominations into formal merger discussions. The Leuenberg Agreement (1973) established full communion among Protestant churches across Europe. The Baptism, Eucharist and Ministry document of 1982 represented decades of patient theological dialogue between traditions that had not spoken to each other for centuries. These were genuine accomplishments, and their significance should not be diminished by the institutional decline that followed.

The Golden Age: 1940s to 1960s

Mainline Protestantism reached its zenith in the decades following World War II. Returning veterans married, moved to suburbs, and joined churches in staggering numbers. Between 1945 and 1960, church membership in the United States grew faster than the population itself. The Methodist Church alone had over eleven million members by 1965. The Presbyterian Church in the U.S.A. peaked at nearly four million. The Episcopal Church, though smaller, wielded influence wildly disproportionate to its size, producing presidents, Supreme Court justices, and Wall Street titans.

This was the era of what sociologist Will Herberg described in his 1955 book Protestant-Catholic-Jew: a tripartite American civil religion in which to be a good American meant belonging to one of these three traditions. And among the three, Protestantism, specifically mainline Protestantism, was first among equals. It set the cultural tone. Its ministers appeared on the cover of Time magazine. Its theologians, Reinhold Niebuhr chief among them, were consulted by presidents and cited in foreign policy debates. Niebuhr's The Irony of American History (1952) remains one of the most penetrating analyses of American power ever written, and it was composed by a man whose primary vocation was preaching.

The National Council of Churches, the institutional expression of mainline Protestant cooperation, functioned as a quasi-official religious voice of the nation. Its pronouncements on race, poverty, and international affairs carried weight in Washington. Its member denominations ran some of the largest charitable and educational operations in the country. The mainline was not merely a religious phenomenon. It was a civilizational one.

Theological Liberalism: What It Actually Is

To understand the mainline, one must understand liberal theology, a term almost universally misused in popular discourse. Theological liberalism is not simply "being progressive on social issues." It is a specific intellectual tradition with identifiable founders, methods, and commitments.

The tradition begins with Friedrich Schleiermacher (1768-1834), often called the father of liberal theology. Writing in the wake of the Enlightenment, Schleiermacher argued that religion should not be reduced to doctrine or morality but understood as rooted in a "feeling of absolute dependence," a pre-cognitive experience of the infinite. This move was revolutionary. It grounded religion not in propositions about God but in human experience of the divine. Critics, then and now, argue that this effectively made human subjectivity the measure of theology.

Paul Tillich (1886-1965) pushed this further, defining God not as a being among beings but as "the ground of being," the depth dimension of all reality. Tillich's method of correlation sought to connect the questions arising from human existence with the answers provided by Christian symbols. The cross, for example, was not merely a historical event but a symbol of the courage to accept meaninglessness. This was extraordinarily sophisticated philosophy. It was also, for many laypeople, almost entirely unintelligible.

Rudolf Bultmann (1884-1976) applied existentialist categories to the New Testament, arguing that the mythological framework of the Gospels, demons, miracles, a three-tiered universe, needed to be "demythologized" to reveal the existential truth beneath. The resurrection, in Bultmann's reading, was not a historical event but an expression of the disciples' experience of new life through the proclaimed word. These ideas filtered through seminary education into mainline pulpits, sometimes carefully, sometimes crudely. A generation of ministers was trained to think critically about Scripture but often lacked the pastoral skill to communicate what remained after criticism had done its work.

The Social Justice Commitment

Whatever its theological complexities, the mainline produced an extraordinary legacy of social engagement. The Social Gospel movement of the early twentieth century, led by figures such as Walter Rauschenbusch, argued that the Kingdom of God was not merely an otherworldly hope but a mandate for transforming unjust social structures. Rauschenbusch's Christianity and the Social Crisis (1907) remains a landmark in the integration of theology and social ethics.

This impulse bore fruit across the century. Mainline churches were among the earliest institutional supporters of the civil rights movement. The National Council of Churches organized clergy to join the 1965 Selma to Montgomery marches. Episcopal seminarians were among the murdered civil rights workers in the South. Mainline denominations issued early statements against the Vietnam War, often at significant cost to their internal unity. They ordained women decades before evangelicalism would even consider the question: the Methodist Church in 1956, the Presbyterian Church in 1956, the Lutheran Church in America in 1970.

The mainline's commitment to racial justice, economic equality, and peace was not an aberration or a capitulation to secular liberalism. It flowed from a genuine, if debatable, reading of the prophetic tradition. Amos, Isaiah, and Micah demanded justice. Jesus proclaimed good news to the poor. The question was never whether the church should care about justice. The question was whether justice commitments had become a substitute for everything else the church was supposed to be.

The Demographic Collapse

The numbers tell a story that is difficult to dispute. In 1965, mainline Protestant denominations claimed roughly 40 percent of the American population. By 2020, that figure had fallen below 10 percent. The United Methodist Church lost nearly four million members between 1970 and 2020, even before the schism over sexuality that would accelerate the decline. The Presbyterian Church (U.S.A.) fell from 4.2 million members in 1965 to under 1.2 million by 2023. The Episcopal Church dropped from 3.6 million to approximately 1.6 million. The United Church of Christ fell from 2 million to under 800,000. The Disciples of Christ went from nearly 1.9 million to around 300,000.

These are not marginal declines. They represent a demographic catastrophe. Entire conferences and synods have closed. Historic churches with century-old endowments have shuttered their doors. Seminary enrollments have plummeted. The average age of a mainline Protestant in the United States is now well above sixty. In some denominations, the median age of clergy exceeds the median age of the congregation, a statistical impossibility in a healthy institution.

Multiple factors converged. Birth rates among mainline Protestants dropped sharply after the 1960s, tracking closely with education and income levels. The baby boom generation, raised in these churches, left in enormous numbers during the cultural upheavals of the late 1960s and 1970s and never returned. Their children were often not baptized, not catechized, and not formed in any tradition at all. Meanwhile, evangelical and Pentecostal churches, with their higher birth rates, more aggressive evangelism, and clearer theological boundaries, grew rapidly, often absorbing former mainline members who wanted something more definite than what the mainline offered.

Why They Declined

The causes of mainline decline are debated, but several factors recur in nearly every analysis. The sociologist Dean Kelley, himself a mainline Protestant, argued in his influential 1972 book Why Conservative Churches Are Growing that strict churches, those demanding clear commitment and maintaining sharp boundaries, thrive, while lenient churches, those accommodating to the surrounding culture and lowering barriers to entry, decline. Kelley's thesis was uncomfortable precisely because it came from within the mainline world.

The theologian Thomas Oden, once a committed theological liberal, argued that the mainline had made a Faustian bargain: it had gained cultural respectability by abandoning theological distinctiveness. When the culture moved on, there was nothing left to hold people. If the church's message was indistinguishable from the editorial page of The New York Times, why get up early on Sunday?

The sociologists Roger Finke and Rodney Stark, in The Churching of America (1992), applied economic models to American religion and concluded that mainline decline was predictable: religious organizations that reduce the "cost" of membership, that ask little and offer vague spiritual uplift, lose market share to groups that demand more and deliver a clearer product. This language offends ecclesiological sensibilities, but the pattern it describes has been remarkably consistent across three centuries of American religious history.

There is also the simple matter of institutional sclerosis. Mainline denominations developed enormous bureaucracies during their years of growth. Those bureaucracies proved resistant to reform and slow to adapt. National offices issued statements on geopolitics while local churches struggled to pay heating bills. The gap between denominational elites and congregational life widened into a chasm.

The Conservative Critique and the Progressive Defense

The conservative critique is blunt and not entirely wrong: the mainline accommodated to the culture until there was nothing distinctive left to join. It replaced the scandal of the gospel with the respectability of progressive politics. It trained ministers to deconstruct the faith but not to proclaim it. It confused relevance with faithfulness and discovered too late that a church indistinguishable from a progressive nonprofit has no reason to exist as a church.

The progressive defense is more nuanced and also not entirely wrong: the mainline followed the Spirit where it led, even when that meant challenging comfortable orthodoxies. It ordained women when others refused. It welcomed divorced people when others shunned them. It spoke against racism when other churches sanctified it. It opposed unjust wars when other churches wrapped the cross in the flag. If faithfulness means following Jesus into uncomfortable places, the mainline has a record worth defending.

The truth, as is often the case, is more complex than either side admits. The mainline's social witness was frequently prophetic. Its theological seriousness produced some of the finest scholarship in Christian history. But it also suffered from a fatal inability to articulate why any of this required a church. Justice work can be done by secular organizations. Intellectual inquiry can be pursued at universities. Community can be found in clubs, neighborhoods, and online networks. What the church uniquely offers, encounter with the living God, proclamation of a story that reframes all other stories, formation in practices that shape the soul, the mainline increasingly struggled to deliver with conviction.

What Mainline Decline Means

The decline of mainline Protestantism is not merely a denominational problem. It is a cultural one. These institutions mediated between faith and reason, between tradition and modernity, between piety and public responsibility. Their disappearance leaves a vacuum that has been filled by two inadequate alternatives: a fundamentalism that refuses engagement with modern thought, and a secularism that refuses engagement with transcendence.

The mainline, at its best, insisted that one could be intellectually honest and spiritually serious, theologically informed and socially engaged, rooted in tradition and open to reform. That combination is rare and precious, and its loss impoverishes not just Christianity but American public life.

Can They Survive?

The case against survival is statistical and institutional. Aging congregations, declining giving, deferred building maintenance, seminary debt, clergy shortages in rural areas, and the departure of entire congregations over theological disputes, these trends have compounding effects that are extremely difficult to reverse. Some scholars predict that several mainline denominations will cease to exist as national institutions within two decades.

The case for survival is theological and adaptive. Mainline traditions carry liturgical depth, intellectual seriousness, and institutional memory that cannot be easily replicated. Some congregations are experiencing renewal through liturgical recovery, community engagement, and a willingness to be smaller but more intentional. The Benedictine option, small communities of serious practice, may be the mainline's unexpected future.

There are also signs of unexpected vitality in particular congregations that have abandoned the model of the large, program-driven church and embraced a more monastic or missional identity. Churches like the Church of the Saviour in Washington, D.C., founded by Gordon Cosby in 1947, pioneered a model of small, intensely committed communities oriented around both inward spiritual formation and outward mission to the poor. This model has influenced a generation of church planters, many of whom draw on mainline traditions while abandoning mainline institutional assumptions.

What is certain is that the mainline will not return to cultural dominance. That era is over. The question is whether these traditions can find a way to be faithful without being powerful, relevant without being indistinguishable from the culture, and prophetic without being self-righteous. It is, in some ways, the question facing all of American Christianity. The mainline is simply encountering it first.
excerpt: For most of the twentieth century, mainline Protestantism was American Christianity. Its decline is not merely a story about shrinking pews. It is a story about what happens when a faith tradition succeeds so completely at shaping a culture that it can no longer distinguish itself from it.

title: What Evangelicalism Was Supposed to Be
body:
The word "evangelical" comes from the Greek euangelion, meaning "good news" or "gospel." In its oldest usage, it simply described anyone who took the gospel message seriously. Martin Luther used the term to describe churches shaped by the Reformation. In much of Europe, "evangelical" remains a synonym for "Protestant." The word carries no political connotation in Germany, Brazil, or South Korea. It is only in the United States that "evangelical" has come to mean something that would be unrecognizable to its founders.

The story of how that happened is a story about good intentions, institutional ambition, cultural anxiety, and the seductive power of political access. It is also a cautionary tale about what happens when a theological identity becomes a tribal one.

The Four Marks: The Bebbington Quadrilateral

The historian David Bebbington, in his landmark 1989 study Evangelicalism in Modern Britain, identified four defining characteristics of evangelical Christianity. These have become the standard scholarly framework, known as the Bebbington Quadrilateral.

The first is conversionism: the belief that lives need to be changed through a conscious, personal encounter with Jesus Christ. This is not merely intellectual assent to doctrines but a transformative experience, what evangelicals have historically called being "born again." The second is activism: the conviction that the gospel must be expressed in effort, particularly in evangelism and social reform. Faith is not private contemplation but public witness. The third is biblicism: a particular regard for the Bible as the ultimate authority in matters of faith and practice. The fourth is crucicentrism: a focus on the atoning work of Christ on the cross as the center of the gospel message.

Notice what is absent from this list. There is no mention of a political party. No reference to a position on immigration, gun rights, or tax policy. No cultural aesthetic. No racial or national identity. The Bebbington Quadrilateral describes a theological orientation, not a voting bloc. That distinction would prove impossible to maintain.

Carl Henry and the Uneasy Conscience

Modern American evangelicalism was born in deliberate reaction against fundamentalism. The fundamentalist movement of the early twentieth century had successfully defended several core Christian doctrines against liberal theology, including the virgin birth, the bodily resurrection, and the authority of Scripture. But it had done so at enormous cost. By the 1940s, fundamentalism had become intellectually isolationist, culturally separatist, and often belligerently anti-modern. Fundamentalist institutions discouraged engagement with secular universities, mainstream media, and the broader culture. The faith was defended by withdrawal.

Carl F. H. Henry, a young theologian and journalist, saw this as a betrayal of the gospel's own logic. In 1947, he published The Uneasy Conscience of Modern Fundamentalism, a slim but explosive book that argued fundamentalism had abandoned the social implications of the gospel. Henry contended that evangelical Christianity had a responsibility not only to save souls but to address the great social evils of the day: racism, poverty, injustice. A gospel that had nothing to say about the world God loved was, Henry argued, an incomplete gospel.

Henry's book was not a call to political liberalism. It was a call to intellectual and social seriousness rooted in orthodox theology. He wanted evangelicals to engage the culture without capitulating to it, to be in the world but not of it, to bring the full resources of Christian thought to bear on public life. This was the founding vision. It was ambitious, noble, and extraordinarily difficult to sustain.

Billy Graham and the Institutional Project

If Henry provided the intellectual framework, Billy Graham provided the charisma and organizational genius. Graham's crusades, beginning in the late 1940s, drew enormous crowds and brought evangelical Christianity into the American mainstream. Graham was handsome, articulate, and media-savvy. He preached a simple gospel message, conversion through faith in Christ, with emotional power and theatrical staging that made him a cultural phenomenon.

But Graham's significance extended far beyond his preaching. In 1956, he founded Christianity Today, a magazine intended to be the evangelical alternative to the liberal Christian Century. Henry served as its first editor. The magazine was explicitly designed to demonstrate that evangelical Christianity could be intellectually rigorous, culturally engaged, and theologically grounded. For a generation, it largely succeeded.

Graham also helped establish Fuller Theological Seminary in 1947, conceived as a graduate-level institution that would train evangelical scholars capable of competing with their mainline counterparts at Harvard, Yale, and Union. Fuller represented the evangelical aspiration to intellectual respectability without theological compromise. Its early faculty included serious scholars like Edward John Carnell, who argued that evangelical theology could meet the standards of academic philosophy.

The National Association of Evangelicals (NAE), founded in 1942, served as the organizational counterpart to the mainline's National Council of Churches. The NAE brought together denominations and parachurch organizations that shared evangelical convictions but rejected fundamentalist separatism. It represented a "third way" between fundamentalism and liberalism, orthodox in theology but engaged with the modern world.

The Evangelical Academy

The institutional project extended beyond media and organizing. Evangelical scholars in the mid-twentieth century undertook a serious effort to establish academic credibility. George Eldon Ladd at Fuller Seminary produced New Testament scholarship that earned respect in mainstream academic circles. F.F. Bruce at the University of Manchester demonstrated that evangelical conviction and rigorous historical scholarship were not mutually exclusive. The founding of the Evangelical Theological Society in 1949 created a professional guild for scholars committed to the authority of Scripture but willing to engage the full range of critical methods.

This academic project mattered because it represented an attempt to hold together what modern culture had torn apart: intellectual rigor and spiritual conviction, critical inquiry and confessional commitment. The evangelical scholars of the 1950s and 1960s believed, with some justification, that liberal theology had sacrificed too much in its accommodation to the Enlightenment, but that fundamentalism had sacrificed too much in its refusal to engage with it. They sought a third way, and for a time, they found it. The tragedy is that the movement's institutional center of gravity would shift away from the academy and toward the television studio, the political action committee, and the megachurch platform.

Francis Schaeffer and the Turn Toward Culture War

The pivot came in the 1970s, and one figure looms large in the transition: Francis Schaeffer. A Presbyterian minister and philosopher who ran a Christian community called L'Abri in Switzerland, Schaeffer had spent decades arguing that Western civilization was in decline because it had abandoned its Christian foundations. His books, including The God Who Is There (1968) and How Should We Then Live? (1976), traced a narrative of cultural decline from the Enlightenment through modern art, philosophy, and theology.

Schaeffer's analysis was often more sweeping than careful, painting with a broad brush across complex intellectual history. But his 1979 collaboration with the future surgeon general C. Everett Koop on the film and book series Whatever Happened to the Human Race? marked a decisive turning point. The project focused on abortion, infanticide, and euthanasia, framing them as symptoms of a civilization that had lost its Christian moorings. Schaeffer argued that evangelical Christians had a moral obligation not merely to preach the gospel but to engage in direct political action to defend the sanctity of life.

This was a fateful shift. Henry had called for social engagement rooted in a comprehensive theological vision. Schaeffer called for political mobilization around specific moral issues. The difference is subtle but significant. Henry envisioned evangelicals as thoughtful participants in the full range of public life. Schaeffer's legacy, whatever his intentions, was a movement increasingly defined by opposition to specific cultural developments: abortion, secularism, sexual liberation, and later, same-sex marriage.

The Moral Majority and Political Capture

Jerry Falwell Sr. founded the Moral Majority in 1979, the same year Schaeffer's anti-abortion work was gaining traction. The timing was not coincidental. Republican strategist Paul Weyrich and others had recognized that evangelical Christians, historically reluctant to engage in partisan politics, represented an enormous untapped voting bloc. The key was finding issues that could mobilize them.

Contrary to popular memory, the initial catalyst was not abortion but the defense of racially segregated Christian schools. The IRS's decision in 1971 to revoke the tax-exempt status of Bob Jones University for its racial policies galvanized conservative Christians who saw it as government overreach into religious institutions. Abortion was grafted onto this mobilization later, largely through Schaeffer's influence. The Southern Baptist Convention, the largest evangelical denomination, had actually passed a resolution in 1971 supporting the legalization of abortion in certain circumstances. It was only in the late 1970s that abortion became the defining evangelical political issue.

The Moral Majority and its successors, the Christian Coalition led by Ralph Reed, the Family Research Council, Focus on the Family, effectively fused evangelical identity with Republican Party politics. This fusion was spectacularly successful in electoral terms. Evangelical voters became the most reliable Republican constituency. But the cost was enormous. Evangelical Christianity became, in the public imagination, a political movement rather than a theological tradition. The Bebbington Quadrilateral was replaced by a voter guide.

The Scandal of the Evangelical Mind

In 1994, the historian Mark Noll, himself an evangelical scholar of impeccable credentials, published The Scandal of the Evangelical Mind. The book's famous opening line was devastating: "The scandal of the evangelical mind is that there is not much of an evangelical mind." Noll argued that evangelicalism had systematically failed to develop a serious intellectual tradition. It had produced gifted preachers and effective organizers but few scholars, artists, or public intellectuals of the first rank.

Noll traced this failure to several sources: the populist anti-intellectualism of revivalism, the dispensationalist theology that devalued engagement with the present world, and the pragmatism that valued what "worked" over what was true. The result was a movement that was theologically shallow, culturally reactive, and intellectually incurious, exactly the opposite of what Henry and Graham had envisioned.

The irony was piercing. The movement that had been founded to rescue conservative Christianity from fundamentalist anti-intellectualism had reproduced that anti-intellectualism in a new form. It had megachurches instead of storefront churches, bestselling books instead of mimeographed tracts, television networks instead of radio stations. But the intellectual depth that Henry had called for remained conspicuously absent.

The Trump Era and the Identity Crisis

The 2016 presidential election brought the contradictions of American evangelicalism into the open with a force that surprised even close observers. Eighty-one percent of white evangelicals voted for Donald Trump, a thrice-married casino mogul who could not name a favorite Bible verse and whose personal conduct violated every standard that evangelical leaders had championed for decades. The leaders who had insisted that "character counts" during the Clinton impeachment suddenly discovered that character was secondary to Supreme Court appointments.

This was not hypocrisy in the simple sense. It was something more revealing. It exposed the degree to which "evangelical" had become a cultural and political identity rather than a theological one. Researchers found that many people who identified as "evangelical" in surveys rarely attended church and could not articulate basic Christian doctrines. They were using "evangelical" as a marker of white, conservative, rural or suburban cultural identity, not a description of their relationship to the euangelion.

The aftermath was a fracture. Prominent evangelical leaders like Russell Moore, then head of the Southern Baptist Convention's Ethics and Religious Liberty Commission, criticized the uncritical embrace of Trump and faced fierce backlash from within the denomination. Younger evangelicals, particularly those of color, began abandoning the label in droves. The historian Thomas Kidd published Who Is an Evangelical? (2019), attempting to recover the historical meaning of the term. Multiple evangelical leaders and scholars publicly renounced the label, not because they had changed their theology but because the word no longer meant what they meant by it.

The Megachurch and the Market

Running parallel to the political capture of evangelicalism was a transformation in its institutional form. The megachurch movement, which exploded in the 1980s and 1990s, represented the marriage of evangelical theology (or at least evangelical aesthetics) with consumer capitalism. Churches like Willow Creek Community Church, founded by Bill Hybels in 1975, and Saddleback Church, founded by Rick Warren in 1980, pioneered the "seeker-sensitive" model: remove the barriers that make unchurched people uncomfortable (hymnals, liturgy, religious symbolism, guilt), and offer a product that meets felt needs (practical sermons, professional music, convenient parking, excellent childcare).

The megachurch model worked spectacularly in numerical terms. By the early 2000s, there were over 1,200 megachurches (defined as congregations with weekly attendance exceeding 2,000) in the United States, the vast majority evangelical or charismatic. But the model also accelerated the transformation of evangelicalism from a theological tradition into a consumer experience. When the church is designed around the preferences of the religious consumer, the consumer's preferences inevitably shape the theology. The hard edges of the gospel, repentance, sacrifice, the cost of discipleship, were sanded down in favor of messages about personal fulfillment, relational health, and financial success. Joel Osteen, whose Lakewood Church in Houston draws over 40,000 weekly, represents the logical endpoint of this trajectory: Christianity as therapeutic optimism, with the cross barely visible behind the smile.

Who Still Claims the Label?

The evangelical world has splintered into at least three identifiable groups. The first is the political-cultural bloc: predominantly white, Republican-aligned, and increasingly defined by opposition to progressive cultural change rather than by theological conviction. This group is numerically dominant and controls most of the movement's institutional infrastructure. The second is the "post-evangelical" contingent: people formed in evangelical churches who retain some evangelical convictions but reject the political and cultural captivity of the movement. Many have migrated to mainline, Anglican, or Catholic traditions, or to independent churches that avoid the evangelical label. The third is the global evangelical movement: churches in Africa, Latin America, and Asia that hold evangelical theological convictions but have no connection to American partisan politics and are often baffled by the American conflation of gospel and party.

What Was Lost

What was lost when evangelicalism became a political identity is precisely what Carl Henry fought to build: a theologically serious, culturally engaged, intellectually honest Christian witness that was beholden to no party and captive to no ideology. Henry wanted evangelicals to bring the gospel to bear on public life. What happened instead is that public life consumed the gospel. The euangelion became a brand. The good news became a platform. And a movement that began as a call to conscience ended as a call to vote.

The recovery of what evangelicalism was supposed to be would require something that movements are rarely capable of: institutional humility, theological self-examination, and the willingness to lose cultural power for the sake of spiritual integrity. Whether that recovery is possible, or whether "evangelical" is now permanently a political word with a thin theological veneer, may be the most consequential question in American Christianity today.

Henry's Uneasy Conscience was prophetic in ways he could not have imagined. The conscience he tried to awaken has been anesthetized by power. Whether it can be revived depends not on elections or institutions but on whether enough people still believe that the good news is more important than the news cycle.
excerpt: Evangelicalism was born as a reform movement, an attempt to rescue Protestant Christianity from both the anti-intellectualism of fundamentalism and the theological drift of liberalism. That it became something else entirely is one of the great tragedies of modern American religion.

title: The Black Church: The Most Important Institution in American Christianity
body:
There is no single institution in American history that has done more with fewer resources, under greater oppression, with less recognition, than the Black church. It educated a people when education was illegal. It organized a community when organization was punishable by death. It produced a theology of liberation a century before European theologians gave it a name. And it did all of this while white Christianity, with rare exceptions, either ignored it, opposed it, or patronized it.

To understand the Black church is to understand that it was never merely a religious institution. It was the school, the bank, the political caucus, the mutual aid society, the concert hall, and the courtroom of a people systematically excluded from every other institution in American life. The church was the one place where Black Americans could be fully human, fully vocal, and fully free. That this institution was built on a faith given to them by their enslavers, and then transformed into something their enslavers could not recognize, is one of the most remarkable feats of theological creativity in the history of Christianity.

The Invisible Institution

The religious life of enslaved Africans in America began in secrecy and subversion. Slaveholders had a complicated relationship with the Christianization of enslaved people. Some believed, or claimed to believe, that baptism conferred freedom, which made them reluctant to allow it. Others promoted a carefully controlled version of Christianity that emphasized obedience: "Slaves, obey your masters" (Ephesians 6:5) was the most frequently cited verse on the plantation. The Christianity offered to enslaved people was a theology of submission, designed to baptize the existing order and render resistance sinful.

The enslaved did not accept this theology. In what historian Albert Raboteau called "the invisible institution," enslaved people gathered in secret, in woods and hollows, in what came to be known as "hush arbors" or "brush arbors," spaces concealed from the surveillance of the slaveholder. There, beyond the reach of the master's Christianity, they developed their own theology, their own worship practices, and their own reading of Scripture.

And they read Scripture differently. Where the slaveholder saw Paul's injunction to obedience, the enslaved saw the Exodus. The God of the Bible was not the God of the plantation chapel, a deity who sanctioned hierarchy and demanded compliance. The God of the hush arbor was the God who heard the cry of the oppressed, who sent Moses to Pharaoh, who parted the sea, who brought down the mighty and lifted up the lowly. This was not an incidental difference in interpretation. It was a fundamentally different encounter with the text, born of a fundamentally different social location.

The Spirituals: Theology Encoded in Music

The spirituals were not merely songs. They were systematic theology set to music, encoded communication, and survival strategy rolled into one. When enslaved people sang "Go Down, Moses," they were not performing a quaint folk melody. They were articulating a theology of liberation: God intervenes in history on behalf of the oppressed. Pharaoh is not merely an ancient Egyptian ruler. Pharaoh is the slaveholder. Egypt is not merely a historical location. Egypt is the plantation. The promised land is not merely Canaan. The promised land is freedom.

"Wade in the Water" functioned simultaneously as worship and practical instruction: escaping enslaved people should walk through water to throw off the scent for tracking dogs. "Steal Away to Jesus" was both a hymn of spiritual longing and a signal that a secret meeting was being called. "Swing Low, Sweet Chariot" may have referenced the Underground Railroad. The genius of the spirituals was their double meaning: they could be sung openly because their surface meaning was pious, while their deeper meaning was revolutionary.

W.E.B. Du Bois recognized this in The Souls of Black Folk (1903), devoting his final chapter to "The Sorrow Songs." Du Bois heard in the spirituals "the singular spiritual heritage of the nation and the greatest gift of the Negro people," a music that carried the full weight of suffering, faith, resistance, and hope. The spirituals were the first original American contribution to world Christianity, and they came not from the seminaries of the powerful but from the fields of the enslaved.

Richard Allen and the Institutional Church

The transition from invisible institution to visible institution is embodied in the life of Richard Allen (1760-1831). Born enslaved in Philadelphia, Allen converted to Methodism, purchased his freedom, and became a licensed preacher. He worshipped at St. George's Methodist Episcopal Church in Philadelphia until 1787, when he and other Black congregants were physically pulled from their knees during prayer for sitting in seats that white members claimed. Allen walked out and never returned.

In 1794, Allen founded Bethel African Methodist Episcopal Church in Philadelphia. In 1816, he established the African Methodist Episcopal (AME) Church as an independent denomination, the first major religious denomination in the Western world founded by and for Black people. The AME Church was not merely a religious organization. It was a declaration of institutional independence, a refusal to accept spiritual equality in theory while enduring physical humiliation in practice.

Other denominations followed. The African Methodist Episcopal Zion Church was organized in 1821. Black Baptist churches, which had existed independently since the late eighteenth century, organized into state and national conventions throughout the nineteenth century, eventually forming the National Baptist Convention in 1895, which remains the largest African American religious organization in the United States. These institutions became the infrastructure of Black communal life in America.

The Center of Community Life

After Emancipation, the Black church became the primary institution around which freed Black communities organized themselves. In an America that systematically excluded Black people from political participation, economic opportunity, and educational access, the church filled every gap.

It was the school: Black churches established some of the earliest schools for freed people. Many historically Black colleges and universities, including Morehouse, Spelman, Fisk, and Howard, have roots in church-sponsored education. It was the bank: when formal financial institutions refused to serve Black communities, church-based mutual aid societies, burial societies, and lending circles provided economic infrastructure. It was the political forum: in a society where Black political expression was suppressed by violence, the church was the one institution where leadership could be developed, oratory could be practiced, and organizing could occur with some degree of safety. It was the cultural center: the Black church produced musicians, writers, artists, and intellectuals who shaped American culture far beyond the boundaries of the congregation.

The sociologist E. Franklin Frazier described the Black church as "a nation within a nation," and the phrase is not hyperbolic. For a people denied the full benefits of American citizenship, the church provided an alternative civic structure, complete with its own leaders, its own social services, its own educational system, and its own moral authority.

A Liberation Theology Before Liberation Theology

When Gustavo Gutierrez published A Theology of Liberation in 1971, launching the academic field of liberation theology, he was systematizing insights that the Black church had been practicing for two centuries. The enslaved did not need a European-educated Peruvian priest to tell them that God takes sides with the oppressed. They had read Exodus. They had sung the spirituals. They had built institutions of resistance and survival on the theological conviction that the God of Jesus Christ is not neutral in the face of injustice.

This theology was not written in academic treatises. It was preached from pulpits, sung in choirs, and lived in daily acts of resistance and mutual care. It was a theology of practice before it was a theology of theory. And it was profoundly orthodox in ways that its critics often failed to recognize. The Black church did not embrace liberation theology as a departure from traditional Christianity. It understood liberation as the meaning of traditional Christianity. The God who freed Israel from Egypt, who announced good news to the poor through Jesus, who raised the crucified one from the dead, was a God whose very nature was oriented toward the liberation of the oppressed.

The Civil Rights Movement as a Church Movement

The civil rights movement of the 1950s and 1960s was, at its core, a church movement. This fact has been so thoroughly secularized in popular memory that many Americans do not fully grasp it. Martin Luther King Jr. was not a political activist who happened to be a minister. He was a minister whose activism was an expression of his theology. His nonviolent philosophy was grounded in a synthesis of the Social Gospel, Gandhian nonviolence, and the Black church tradition of prophetic witness. His rhetoric was sermonic. His organizing structure was ecclesial. The Southern Christian Leadership Conference was a coalition of ministers. The mass meetings were worship services. The freedom songs were spirituals and hymns adapted for a new moment of liberation.

Fannie Lou Hamer, who helped organize the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party and challenged the segregationist delegation at the 1964 Democratic National Convention, was a church woman whose courage was rooted in her faith. When she testified before the credentials committee, she quoted Scripture. When she was beaten in a Winona, Mississippi, jail, she sang hymns. Her famous declaration, "I'm sick and tired of being sick and tired," was not secular frustration. It was prophetic lament.

John Lewis, who would serve in Congress for three decades, was trained in nonviolent resistance at workshops organized by the Nashville Christian Leadership Council. His concept of "good trouble" was theological before it was political. The willingness to absorb violence without retaliation, to suffer for justice, to love one's enemies, these were not merely strategic calculations. They were spiritual disciplines rooted in the cross.

The civil rights movement was the most successful moral revolution in American history, and it was led, organized, funded, and sustained by the Black church. No other institution, not the federal government, not the academy, not the media, played a comparable role. This is a fact that white American Christianity has never fully reckoned with: the most Christlike movement in American history was organized by the people white Christians had enslaved, segregated, and excluded.

Black Theology: James Cone and the God of the Oppressed

James Cone (1938-2018) gave academic form to what the Black church had always known. His 1969 book Black Theology and Black Power, followed by A Black Theology of Liberation (1970) and God of the Oppressed (1975), argued that theology must be done from the perspective of the oppressed, that the God of the Bible is unambiguously on the side of the marginalized, and that any theology that does not address the reality of racial oppression is not Christian theology at all.

Cone's work was deliberately provocative. He wrote that "Christ is Black" not as a statement about Jesus's physical appearance but as a theological claim: Christ identifies with the oppressed, and in America, the oppressed are disproportionately Black. He challenged white theology's pretension to universality, arguing that all theology is contextual and that white theology's failure to address racism was not neutrality but complicity.

White theologians were scandalized. Many dismissed Cone as a polemicist. But his central claim, that a theology that ignores the suffering of the oppressed is not faithful to the God of the Bible, is difficult to refute on scriptural grounds. The prophets of Israel, Jesus's inaugural sermon in Luke 4, the Magnificat of Mary, the parable of the sheep and the goats, all point toward a God whose concern for the marginalized is not incidental but definitional.

The Prosperity Gospel in Black Churches

The presence of the prosperity gospel in Black churches requires careful analysis that avoids both uncritical acceptance and condescending dismissal. When prosperity theology appears in a community that has been systematically denied economic opportunity for centuries, it carries a different meaning than when it appears in a white suburban megachurch.

For many Black prosperity preachers and their congregations, the message that God wants you to prosper is not merely about individual wealth. It is a theological rejection of the idea that Black poverty is natural, ordained, or permanent. It is an assertion of divine blessing against a history that has systematically communicated the opposite. The theology is problematic, its exegesis strained, its consequences sometimes exploitative. But the impulse behind it, the insistence that God's people deserve abundance and not merely survival, taps into something real and deeply felt.

The critique, and it is a necessary one, is that prosperity theology often individualizes what are structural problems, replacing prophetic analysis of systemic injustice with personal claims on divine favor. It can redirect energy from collective action to individual consumption. And it has made some preachers fabulously wealthy at the expense of congregations that can ill afford it. The tension between prophetic justice and prosperity theology within the Black church is real and ongoing.

Cultural Production: From Gospel to Hip-Hop

The cultural production of the Black church has shaped American culture far beyond the walls of the sanctuary. Gospel music, pioneered by Thomas A. Dorsey in the 1930s and electrified by Mahalia Jackson, the Edwin Hawkins Singers, Andrae Crouch, and Kirk Franklin, became one of the most influential musical traditions in the world. The vocal techniques of gospel, the call-and-response patterns, the emotional intensity, and the improvisational freedom flowed directly into rhythm and blues, soul, and rock and roll. Sam Cooke, Aretha Franklin, Marvin Gaye, Al Green, and Whitney Houston all came out of the church. American popular music is, to a degree rarely acknowledged, secularized Black church music.

Hip-hop's relationship to the Black church is more complicated but no less real. The prophetic tradition of speaking truth to power, of narrating the experience of the marginalized, of bearing witness to suffering and injustice, runs through hip-hop's DNA. Artists from Tupac Shakur to Kendrick Lamar have wrestled publicly with faith, sin, redemption, and divine judgment in ways that mirror the Black preaching tradition. Lamar's DAMN. is, in many ways, a sermon on the problem of theodicy. The church may not always recognize its children, but its influence is unmistakable.

What the White Church Has Never Learned

The white church in America has consistently failed to learn from the Black church, and the failure is not incidental. It is structural. To learn from the Black church would require acknowledging that the most vibrant, most prophetic, most theologically creative tradition in American Christianity emerged not from the centers of institutional power but from the margins, not from the seminaries of the privileged but from the suffering of the enslaved.

The white church has never learned that theology done from a position of comfort is always incomplete. It has never learned that worship disconnected from justice is idolatry. It has never learned that the Bible, read by the oppressed, says things that the powerful cannot hear. It has never learned that the cross is not an abstract doctrine but a political reality, that Jesus was executed by the state, and that any Christianity that consistently aligns with state power has lost the plot.

The Black church tradition insists on what the white church perpetually forgets: that Christianity is a faith born in oppression, proclaimed by the marginalized, and most authentically expressed when it speaks from below rather than from above. This is not a racial claim. It is a theological one. And it stands at the center of the New Testament, waiting to be heard by those with ears to hear.

The Ongoing Prophetic Witness

The Black church in the twenty-first century faces its own crises: generational decline in some denominations, the pull of secularism among younger Black Americans, the tension between traditional social conservatism and progressive politics, and the persistent challenge of ministering to communities devastated by mass incarceration, economic inequality, and police violence. The Movement for Black Lives, while not a church movement in the way the civil rights movement was, drew heavily on the prophetic tradition of the Black church even as it challenged the church's conservatism on issues of gender and sexuality.

But the Black church remains. It remains because it has always been more than a religious institution. It is the institutional expression of a people's determination to survive, to create beauty in the midst of brutality, to find God in the midst of godforsakenness. It is the tradition that took the slaveholder's religion and turned it into a weapon of liberation. It is the tradition that produced the spirituals, the civil rights movement, and a theology of hope that has sustained a people through four centuries of oppression.

Any Christianity that does not reckon with the Black church is an incomplete Christianity. Any theology that does not listen to voices from the underside of history is a parochial theology masquerading as universal truth. The Black church is not a subcategory of American Christianity. It is, in many ways, its most faithful expression.
excerpt: The Black church did not emerge as a branch of American Protestantism. It emerged in spite of it. Born in the crucible of enslavement, sustained through Jim Crow, and central to the most significant moral movement in American history, the Black church is the tradition white Christianity has never adequately reckoned with.

title: Pentecostalism and the Global South
body:
On April 9, 1906, in a converted stable at 312 Azusa Street in Los Angeles, something happened that would reshape global Christianity more profoundly than any event since the Reformation. A small group of worshippers, led by William J. Seymour, a one-eyed Black preacher and the son of former slaves, began speaking in tongues, a phenomenon they identified as the baptism of the Holy Spirit described in Acts 2. The Azusa Street Revival would continue for three years, drawing visitors from around the world who carried its fire back to their home countries. Within a century, the movement it spawned would claim over 600 million adherents worldwide, making Pentecostalism the fastest-growing form of Christianity in human history.

The irony is worth pausing over. The movement that would become the dominant expression of twenty-first-century Christianity was born not in a cathedral or a university but in a former horse stable. It was led not by a credentialed theologian but by a man denied admission to the seminary of his own denomination because of his race. And it was, in its earliest expression, radically interracial, a fact that would be quickly suppressed as American racial ideology reasserted itself.

Azusa Street: The Interracial Origins

William Joseph Seymour (1870-1922) was born in Centerville, Louisiana, to parents who had been enslaved. He was largely self-educated, having been denied formal theological training by Charles Fox Parham's Bible school in Houston, which allowed him to listen to lectures only from the hallway because of his race. Seymour took Parham's teaching on the baptism of the Holy Spirit and transformed it into something Parham never intended: an interracial, egalitarian, Spirit-filled community that violated every social convention of early twentieth-century America.

The Azusa Street Mission was remarkable not only for its spiritual phenomena, speaking in tongues, healings, prophecies, but for its social composition. Black, white, Latino, and Asian worshippers prayed, sang, and fell under the Spirit together in an era when such mixing was both illegal in some jurisdictions and unthinkable in most churches. Frank Bartleman, a white eyewitness, famously wrote that at Azusa Street "the color line was washed away in the blood." This was an overstatement, the racial dynamics were more complex than hagiography suggests, but the aspiration was genuine and the reality, however imperfect, was extraordinary for its time.

The interracial character of early Pentecostalism did not survive. By 1914, when the Assemblies of God was organized as a predominantly white denomination, the movement had already segregated along racial lines. The Church of God in Christ, led by Charles Harrison Mason, became the largest Black Pentecostal denomination. The racial divide in American Pentecostalism mirrored the racial divide in American Christianity more broadly, a failure that haunts the movement to this day.

The Four Waves

Scholars of Pentecostalism typically identify four waves or phases of the movement. The first wave is classical Pentecostalism, the denominational tradition that emerged directly from Azusa Street and its precursors. This includes the Assemblies of God, the Church of God in Christ, the Church of God (Cleveland, Tennessee), the International Church of the Foursquare Gospel (founded by Aimee Semple McPherson), and numerous smaller bodies. These denominations are characterized by a distinct theology of "subsequence": the baptism of the Holy Spirit is understood as an experience subsequent to and distinct from conversion, evidenced by speaking in tongues.

The second wave is the charismatic renewal movement that emerged in the 1960s and 1970s within mainline Protestant and Roman Catholic churches. Episcopal priest Dennis Bennett's 1960 announcement that he had received the gift of tongues is often cited as the beginning of the charismatic movement in mainline Protestantism. The Catholic Charismatic Renewal, which began at Duquesne University in 1967, eventually claimed tens of millions of adherents worldwide. These movements adopted Pentecostal spiritual practices while remaining within their existing denominational structures.

The third wave, identified by C. Peter Wagner in the 1980s, encompasses neo-charismatic movements that emphasize signs and wonders, spiritual warfare, and the continuation of apostolic gifts but do not necessarily identify as Pentecostal or charismatic. The Vineyard movement, founded by John Wimber, is a prominent example. The fourth and most consequential wave consists of independent and indigenous Pentecostal-type movements in the Global South that have no organizational connection to Western Pentecostal denominations but share their emphasis on the immediate experience of the Holy Spirit, healing, deliverance, and exuberant worship.

The Explosive Growth

The numbers are staggering. In 1900, there were essentially no Pentecostals. By 1970, the combined Pentecostal and charismatic movement numbered perhaps 70 million. By 2000, estimates ranged from 400 to 500 million. By 2025, the number exceeds 600 million by most scholarly estimates, with some projections suggesting it could reach 800 million or more by mid-century. If Pentecostal and charismatic Christians were a single denomination, they would constitute the second-largest Christian tradition in the world, behind only Roman Catholicism.

The growth is concentrated overwhelmingly in the Global South. In Latin America, Pentecostalism has transformed the religious landscape. Brazil alone has an estimated 50 to 60 million Pentecostals, and the proportion continues to grow. Guatemala has become majority Protestant, primarily Pentecostal. Chile, Argentina, Colombia, and Mexico have experienced massive Pentecostal growth. In sub-Saharan Africa, Pentecostal and charismatic churches have exploded across the continent, from Nigeria (where the Redeemed Christian Church of God claims over 10 million members) to South Africa, Kenya, Ghana, and the Democratic Republic of Congo. In East Asia, the world's largest congregation, Yoido Full Gospel Church in Seoul, South Korea, is Pentecostal, with a membership that has exceeded 800,000.

Why Pentecostalism Grows

Multiple explanations have been offered for this extraordinary growth, and no single factor suffices. But several recur across contexts and scholarly analyses.

First, Pentecostalism prioritizes experience over doctrine. One need not understand Trinitarian theology or be able to parse the Nicene Creed to receive the Holy Spirit. Pentecostal worship is participatory, emotional, and immediately accessible. You do not need literacy to speak in tongues, clap your hands, or be healed. In communities where formal education is limited, this accessibility is enormous.

Second, Pentecostalism takes the spirit world seriously. In much of the Global South, people live in what scholars call an "enchanted" worldview, one in which spiritual forces, both benign and malevolent, are understood as real and active. Western Christianity, shaped by the Enlightenment, has largely demythologized the spirit world. Pentecostalism has not. It offers prayer for healing, deliverance from demons, and spiritual power in a world where these categories are experientially real to millions of people. It meets people where they are rather than asking them to adopt a Western rationalist framework as a prerequisite for faith.

Third, Pentecostalism builds community and mutual support networks that function as social safety nets in contexts where the state provides little. Pentecostal churches often provide the same services that the Black church provided in the United States: education, economic assistance, healthcare, counseling, and a sense of belonging. For the urban poor migrating from rural areas to megacities like Lagos, Sao Paulo, or Manila, the Pentecostal church offers an instant community, a social network, and a moral framework for navigating a disorienting new environment.

Fourth, Pentecostalism is indigenously adaptable. Unlike Western missionary Christianity, which often came packaged with European cultural forms, liturgies, hymn tunes, architectural styles, and hierarchical structures, Pentecostalism adapts readily to local cultures. Its worship can incorporate local musical traditions, its leadership structures are often flat and entrepreneurial, and its theology, while maintaining certain core commitments, is flexible enough to be reinterpreted in radically different cultural contexts.

Women and Pentecostalism

One of the most significant and underexamined dimensions of Pentecostal growth is the role of women. In many Global South contexts, Pentecostal conversion transforms gender dynamics within families and communities. The emphasis on sobriety, marital fidelity, and male domestic responsibility, values enforced by the Pentecostal community, often benefits women directly. Men who convert to Pentecostalism typically stop drinking, stop womanizing, and redirect income toward the household. The anthropologist Elizabeth Brusco, studying Colombian Pentecostals, described this as a "reformation of machismo" that empowered women even within a formally patriarchal theological framework.

Pentecostalism has also, paradoxically, provided women with public leadership roles that traditional churches denied them. The doctrine that the Holy Spirit distributes gifts without regard to gender has, in practice if not always in theory, opened space for women to preach, prophesy, plant churches, and lead ministries. Aimee Semple McPherson, who founded the International Church of the Foursquare Gospel in 1923, was one of the most famous religious leaders in American history, male or female. In the Global South, women serve as pastors, evangelists, and denominational leaders in numbers that would astonish observers accustomed to the gender hierarchies of traditional Christianity. The Spirit, it turns out, is a more effective feminist than any theological argument.

David Martin's Thesis

The British sociologist David Martin, in his influential 2002 study Pentecostalism: The World Their Parish, argued that Pentecostalism represents the completion of a Reformation that classical Protestantism left unfinished. Luther and Calvin democratized theology, taking it out of the exclusive hands of the priestly caste and making it available to the literate layperson. But they still required literacy, education, and engagement with complex doctrinal systems. Pentecostalism goes further: it democratizes the experience of God itself, making the divine available to anyone, regardless of education, social status, or theological training.

Martin also argued that Pentecostalism functions as a form of cultural modernization, providing converts with the discipline, sobriety, mutual accountability, and work ethic that Max Weber associated with the "Protestant ethic." In Latin America especially, Pentecostal conversion often correlates with the abandonment of alcohol, the stabilization of family life, the development of small business, and upward economic mobility. This does not mean Pentecostalism is merely a vehicle for capitalist self-improvement, but the social effects are real and documented.

The Tension: Spiritual Power and Theological Thinness

The strengths of Pentecostalism are inseparable from its vulnerabilities. The same emphasis on experience that makes the movement accessible also makes it susceptible to manipulation. If the Holy Spirit is the primary authority, and if discerning the Spirit is a subjective exercise, then the potential for charismatic leaders to claim divine sanction for personal agendas is immense. The history of Pentecostalism is littered with scandals, authoritarianism, and financial exploitation by leaders who claimed to speak for God.

The theological thinness of much Pentecostal Christianity is a genuine concern. The movement has produced relatively few systematic theologians, relatively little sustained engagement with historical Christian thought, and relatively weak institutional checks on doctrinal innovation. This has allowed prosperity theology, dominion theology, and various forms of spiritual entrepreneurialism to flourish under the Pentecostal umbrella. When the primary criterion for truth is "the Spirit told me," the tradition lacks internal mechanisms for self-correction.

Prosperity Theology and the Global South

The prosperity gospel has found extraordinarily fertile ground in the Global South, and the picture is more complex than Western critics typically acknowledge. In contexts of extreme poverty, the message that God wants you to prosper is not merely a self-help gimmick. It is a radical theological claim that poverty is not God's will, that the faithful deserve dignity and material sufficiency, and that spiritual power can overcome structural disadvantage. The theology is often exegetically indefensible, its promises frequently unfulfilled, and its effects sometimes devastating when families give their last resources to prosperity preachers. But the appeal is rooted in real suffering and real hope.

The most problematic expressions of prosperity theology in the Global South involve leaders who live in spectacular wealth while their congregations remain impoverished. Churches that function as extraction mechanisms, demanding tithes and "seed offerings" from people who cannot afford them, represent a genuine form of spiritual exploitation. The challenge for Global South Pentecostalism is developing theological resources to critique prosperity theology from within, without dismissing the legitimate aspirations of the poor.

Pentecostalism and Politics

The political dimensions of Pentecostal growth in the Global South deserve separate attention. In Brazil, the "bancada evangelica," the evangelical caucus in the national congress, has become one of the most powerful political blocs in the country. Pentecostal churches have elected mayors, governors, and senators across Latin America. In Nigeria, Pentecostal leaders wield enormous political influence. In Guatemala, two Pentecostal generals have served as president. The pattern is strikingly similar to the American evangelical trajectory: a movement that begins as spiritual renewal eventually discovers the utility of political power.

The consequences are complex. Pentecostal political engagement in the Global South has sometimes been prophetic, challenging corruption and advocating for the poor. It has also sometimes been reactionary, supporting authoritarian leaders, opposing LGBT rights, and aligning with economic elites whose interests are directly opposed to those of the Pentecostal faithful. The Brazilian election of Jair Bolsonaro in 2018, supported overwhelmingly by Pentecostal voters, echoed the American evangelical embrace of Donald Trump in ways that scholars are still analyzing. The question of whether Pentecostalism can sustain its prophetic energy while wielding political power is not yet answered.

What Western Christianity Must Learn

The growth of Pentecostalism in the Global South presents Western Christianity with an uncomfortable mirror.
